before.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
before.season: Mar-Oct (best Apr-May and fall); voluntary closure Feb 1-Mar 31 for wintering deer; also used for winter snowshoeing

itinerary.cal: Boulder Creek fords and lingering snow on the glacier approach are easiest from mid-July through August; the road to White River Trailhead is normally clear by late May but the glacier itself is best climbed before it opens up too much in late summer.

days.note: From the White River Trailhead (2,300 ft), hike the White River Trail about 4 miles, then turn up the Boulder Creek/Boulder Pass Trail, fording Boulder Creek where it braids into several shallow channels. Camp in the forested basin around 5,600-6,000 ft with a view of Clark Mountain's south side.

days.note: An alpine start from Boulder Basin gains Boulder Pass and the east-ridge bench before dropping onto the Walrus Glacier. Rope up and pick a line up the moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (southern) margin, watching for narrow crevasses, then finish with a Class 3 scramble and a short 45-50 degree snow traverse to the summit block. Reverse the same line back to camp.

before.descent_text: The Scoop does not use CBR's standard single-rappel/scree walk-off (the one used by the West Face and most other summit-block routes) because its line sits well right of that descent gully. Instead parties rappel the route itself: with two 60m ropes tied together, descend via a sequence of natural anchors — slung trees and horns down the crack systems below Launch Ledge — there are no bolts or fixed gear anywhere on the route, by design, so you are relying entirely on what you find or build (extra slings/cord are worth carrying). At roughly 900-1,000 ft (10 pitches) of route length, expect on the order of 6-7 rappels to get back to the basin, though exact station spacing isn't published and will depend on where prior parties' anchors sit; be ready to equalize a natural anchor yourself if a station looks marginal. Watch for rope-snag risk in the corner systems on the crux Scoop pitch and loose rock low in the gully system if you bail before topping out.
before.descent: Rappel with two 60m ropes using natural tree/horn anchors to avoid loose terrain; a shorter single-rope rappel option from a slung horn also exists lower on the formation

before.beta: P1 (5.10): start as for West Face; blocky ledges then a splitter on the left. P2 (5.12a): wild, pumpy movement to 2 bolts leftward, then a splitter finish to a 2-bolt belay. P3 (5.11a): continue up the crack. P4 (5.11c): steep, strenuous moves up an obvious dihedral. P5 (5.11c): grasp a pancake-thin jug flake, move left to a crack, into a pleasant bouldery finish. P6 (5.10a): wandering traverse right, then a slab traverse back left.
pro_tips: P2's bolts protect the leftward crux move — clip early and commit
watch_out: P2 (5.12a) and P4/P5 (5.11c) are sustained and pumpy with limited rest — pace the day

before.approach: This is the approach/scramble route to the col above Colchuck Lake's east side, used to access objectives beyond Colchuck Balanced Rock (notably Dragontail Peak). Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) and hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) 4 miles and 2,280 ft to the lake outlet (2.5-3 hours), the last reliable water. At the lake, take the left fork and stay high on the ridge, avoiding spur trails that drop to the water's edge. Continue to a small dam near the lake's north end and cross the outlet creek at or just below it; pick up the trail on the far side and follow it south roughly 100 yards to a slight clearing with boulders and talus on the left. Ascend the talus, angling slightly left into the woods, and negotiate a brief 3rd/4th-class rock step (using roots/branches as holds). From there the path climbs southward through open, cairned forest for about an hour to the col, which overlooks a boulder-strewn camp area with views of Dragontail and Colchuck peaks — consistent with the route's recorded 2,500 ft of gain.

before.approach: This is not a ground-up approach — 'The Balanced Rock' is the short V2 boulder problem on top of the balanced summit block of Colchuck Balanced Rock itself, at roughly 8,240 ft. It's reached only after climbing one of the peak's technical routes to the summit ridge (most commonly the West Face or Let It Burn, both approached via the Stuart Lake Trailhead/Colchuck Lake Trail and the Aasgard Pass climbers' trail — see those routes for the full trailhead-to-wall approach, roughly 3.5-4 hours). From the summit ridge, a short 3rd/4th-class scramble around the true high point leads to the base of the balanced boulder, where the problem climbs the exposed south-east crimpy arête, about 12 ft tall.
